solution: Here \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{x^2 + xy} = F(x, y)\), and \(F(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \frac{\lambda^2(x^2+y^2)}{\lambda^2(x^2+xy)} = F(x, y)\), so the equation is homogeneous of degree zero. Put \(y = vx\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1+v^2}{1+v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1+v^2-v-v^2}{1+v} = \frac{1-v}{1+v}\). Separating, \(\frac{1+v}{1-v}\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\), and since \(\frac{1+v}{1-v} = \frac{2}{1-v} - 1\) this integrates to \(-2\log|1-v| - v = \log|x| + C\). Putting \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) and using \(1 - \frac{y}{x} = \frac{x-y}{x}\), \(2\log|x-y| + \frac{y}{x} = \log|x| + C\), that is \((x-y)^2 = Cx\,e^{-y/x}\). Differentiating this implicitly returns \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2+y^2}{x^2+xy}\), so it checks. The general solution is \((x-y)^2 = Cx\,e^{-y/x}\).

Here \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+y}{x} = 1 + \frac{y}{x}\), which is a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1 + v\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1\). Separating, \(dv = \frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(v = \log|x| + C\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) gives \(y = x\log|x| + Cx\). Checking, \(y' = \log|x| + 1 + C = 1 + \frac{y}{x}\). The general solution is \(y = x\log|x| + Cx\).

Writing it as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+y}{x-y}\), both \(x+y\) and \(x-y\) are homogeneous of degree 1, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1+v}{1-v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1+v-v+v^2}{1-v} = \frac{1+v^2}{1-v}\). Separating, \(\frac{1-v}{1+v^2}\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\), which integrates to \(\tan^{-1}v - \frac{1}{2}\log(1+v^2) = \log|x| + C\). With \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{y^2}{x^2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\log(x^2+y^2) - \log|x|\), so the \(\log|x|\) terms cancel. Implicit differentiation of the result returns \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x+y}{x-y}\), so it checks. The general solution is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\log(x^2+y^2) + C\).

Writing it as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y^2-x^2}{2xy}\), numerator and denominator are both homogeneous of degree 2, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v^2-1}{2v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v^2-1-2v^2}{2v} = -\frac{1+v^2}{2v}\). Separating, \(\frac{2v}{1+v^2}\,dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(\log(1+v^2) + \log|x| = C\). With \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) this is \(\log\frac{x^2+y^2}{x^2} + \log|x| = C\), i.e. \(\log\frac{x^2+y^2}{|x|} = C\). Implicit differentiation of \(\frac{x^2+y^2}{x}\) confirms \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y^2-x^2}{2xy}\). The general solution is \(x^2 + y^2 = Cx\).

Here \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2 - 2y^2 + xy}{x^2} = 1 - 2\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2 + \frac{y}{x}\), a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1 - 2v^2 + v\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1 - 2v^2\). Separating, \(\frac{dv}{1-2v^2} = \frac{dx}{x}\), and \(\int\frac{dv}{1-2v^2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\frac{1+\sqrt{2}\,v}{1-\sqrt{2}\,v}\right|\). Hence \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\frac{1+\sqrt{2}\,v}{1-\sqrt{2}\,v}\right| = \log|x| + C\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) and multiplying numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{2}\), the general solution is \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\frac{\sqrt{2}\,x + 2y}{\sqrt{2}\,x - 2y}\right| = \log|x| + C\).

Writing it as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{x}\), the right side is homogeneous of degree zero, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\) (take \(x > 0\), so \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2} = x\sqrt{1+v^2}\)): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v + \sqrt{1+v^2}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \sqrt{1+v^2}\). Separating, \(\frac{dv}{\sqrt{1+v^2}} = \frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(\log\left|v + \sqrt{1+v^2}\right| = \log|x| + C\), i.e. \(v + \sqrt{1+v^2} = Cx\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) gives \(\frac{y}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{x} = Cx\). Implicit differentiation confirms the original equation. The general solution is \(y + \sqrt{x^2+y^2} = Cx^2\).

Here \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y\left\{x\cos\frac{y}{x} + y\sin\frac{y}{x}\right\}}{x\left\{y\sin\frac{y}{x} - x\cos\frac{y}{x}\right\}}\); numerator and denominator are both homogeneous of degree 2, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): the \(x^2\) cancels and \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v(v\sin v + \cos v)}{v\sin v - \cos v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v(v\sin v+\cos v) - v(v\sin v-\cos v)}{v\sin v - \cos v} = \frac{2v\cos v}{v\sin v - \cos v}\). Separating, \(\frac{v\sin v - \cos v}{2v\cos v}\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\), i.e. \(\left(\frac{\tan v}{2} - \frac{1}{2v}\right)dv = \frac{dx}{x}\), which integrates to \(-\frac{1}{2}\log|v\cos v| = \log|x| + C\). Hence \(v\cos v = \frac{C_1}{x^2}\); with \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) this gives \(\frac{y}{x}\cos\frac{y}{x} = \frac{C_1}{x^2}\). Implicit differentiation of the result returns the original equation. The general solution is \(xy\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = C\).

Rearranging, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - x\sin\frac{y}{x}}{x} = \frac{y}{x} - \sin\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\), a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v - \sin v\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\sin v\). Separating, \(\operatorname{cosec} v\,dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(\log\left|\tan\frac{v}{2}\right| = -\log|x| + C\), i.e. \(x\tan\frac{v}{2} = C\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) and differentiating implicitly returns \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} - \sin\frac{y}{x}\), so it checks. The general solution is \(x\tan\left(\frac{y}{2x}\right) = C\).

Collecting the \(dy\) terms, \(y\,dx = x\left\{2 - \log\frac{y}{x}\right\}dy\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x\left(2 - \log\frac{y}{x}\right)}\), which depends only on \(\frac{y}{x}\); the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v}{2-\log v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v(\log v - 1)}{2 - \log v}\). Separating, \(\frac{2-\log v}{v(\log v - 1)}\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\). Put \(t = \log v - 1\), so \(dt = \frac{dv}{v}\) and \(2 - \log v = 1-t\): the left side becomes \(\int\left(\frac{1}{t}-1\right)dt = \log|t| - t\). Hence \(\log|\log v - 1| - \log v = \log|x| + C\). With \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), \(\log v + \log|x| = \log|y|\), so \(\log|\log v - 1| - \log|y| = C\). Implicit differentiation of the result returns the original equation. The general solution is \(\log\left|\frac{y}{x}\right| - 1 = Cy\).

Both coefficients are homogeneous of degree zero and involve \(\frac{x}{y}\), so the equation is homogeneous and the substitution to use is \(x = vy\), \(\frac{dx}{dy} = v + y\frac{dv}{dy}\). From the equation, \(\frac{dx}{dy} = -\frac{e^{x/y}\left(1-\frac{x}{y}\right)}{1+e^{x/y}}\), so \(v + y\frac{dv}{dy} = -\frac{e^{v}(1-v)}{1+e^{v}}\), giving \(y\frac{dv}{dy} = \frac{-e^{v}+ve^{v}-v-ve^{v}}{1+e^{v}} = -\frac{v+e^{v}}{1+e^{v}}\). Separating, \(\frac{1+e^{v}}{v+e^{v}}\,dv = -\frac{dy}{y}\), hence \(\log|v+e^{v}| = -\log|y| + C\), i.e. \(y(v+e^{v}) = C\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{x}{y}\) and differentiating implicitly returns the original equation. The general solution is \(x + y\,e^{x/y} = C\).

Writing it as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y-x}{x+y}\), the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v-1}{1+v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v-1-v-v^2}{1+v} = -\frac{1+v^2}{1+v}\). Separating, \(\frac{1+v}{1+v^2}\,dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(\tan^{-1}v + \frac{1}{2}\log(1+v^2) + \log|x| = C\). With \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{y^2}{x^2}\right) + \log|x| = \frac{1}{2}\log(x^2+y^2)\), so \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) + \frac{1}{2}\log(x^2+y^2) = C\). Putting \(y = 1\) when \(x = 1\), \(C = \tan^{-1}1 + \frac{1}{2}\log 2 = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\log 2\). The particular solution is \(\log(x^2+y^2) + 2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} + \log 2\).

Writing it as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{xy+y^2}{x^2}\), the equation is homogeneous of degree 2. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = -(v+v^2)\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = -(v^2+2v) = -v(v+2)\). Separating, \(\frac{dv}{v(v+2)} = -\frac{dx}{x}\), and \(\frac{1}{v(v+2)} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{v+2}\right)\), so \(\frac{1}{2}\log\left|\frac{v}{v+2}\right| = -\log|x| + C\), i.e. \(\frac{v}{v+2} = \frac{K}{x^2}\). With \(v = \frac{y}{x}\) this is \(\frac{y}{y+2x} = \frac{K}{x^2}\), i.e. \(x^2y = K(y+2x)\). Putting \(y = 1\) when \(x = 1\) gives \(1 = 3K\), so \(K = \frac{1}{3}\) and \(3x^2y = y + 2x\). Implicit differentiation confirms \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{xy+y^2}{x^2}\). The particular solution is \(y = \frac{2x}{3x^2-1}\).

Rearranging, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - x\sin^2\frac{y}{x}}{x} = \frac{y}{x} - \sin^2\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\), a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v - \sin^2 v\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\sin^2 v\). Separating, \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 v\,dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(-\cot v = -\log|x| + C\), i.e. \(\cot\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + C_1\). Putting \(y = \frac{\pi}{4}\) when \(x = 1\), \(\cot\frac{\pi}{4} = 1 = 0 + C_1\), so \(C_1 = 1\). The particular solution is \(\cot\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + 1 = \log|ex|\).

Rearranging, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} - \operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\), a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = v - \operatorname{cosec} v\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\operatorname{cosec} v\). Separating, \(\sin v\,dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(-\cos v = -\log|x| + C\), i.e. \(\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + C_1\). Putting \(y = 0\) when \(x = 1\), \(\cos 0 = 1 = 0 + C_1\), so \(C_1 = 1\). The particular solution is \(\cos\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \log|x| + 1 = \log|ex|\).

Rearranging, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2xy+y^2}{2x^2}\), whose numerator and denominator are homogeneous of degree 2, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{2v+v^2}{2} = v + \frac{v^2}{2}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v^2}{2}\). Separating, \(\frac{2\,dv}{v^2} = \frac{dx}{x}\), hence \(-\frac{2}{v} = \log|x| + C\), i.e. \(-\frac{2x}{y} = \log|x| + C\). Putting \(y = 2\) when \(x = 1\) gives \(-1 = 0 + C\), so \(C = -1\) and \(\frac{2x}{y} = 1 - \log|x|\). Implicit differentiation confirms the original equation. The particular solution is \(y = \frac{2x}{1-\log|x|}\), \(x \ne 0\), \(x \ne e\).

The equation is already in the form \(\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\) with \(P = 2\) and \(Q = \sin x\). Integrating factor \(= e^{\int 2\,dx} = e^{2x}\). Then \(y\,e^{2x} = \int e^{2x}\sin x\,dx = \frac{e^{2x}}{5}(2\sin x - \cos x) + C\), using \(\int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx - b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}\). Differentiating the result back gives \(\frac{dy}{dx}+2y = \sin x\), so it checks. The general solution is \(y = \frac{2\sin x - \cos x}{5} + C\,e^{-2x}\).

Here \(P = 3\) and \(Q = e^{-2x}\). Integrating factor \(= e^{\int 3\,dx} = e^{3x}\). Then \(y\,e^{3x} = \int e^{3x}e^{-2x}\,dx = \int e^{x}\,dx = e^{x} + C\). Differentiating the result back gives \(\frac{dy}{dx}+3y = e^{-2x}\), so it checks. The general solution is \(y = e^{-2x} + C\,e^{-3x}\).

Here \(P = \frac{1}{x}\) and \(Q = x^2\). Integrating factor \(= e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx} = e^{\log x} = x\). Then \(y\,x = \int x^2\cdot x\,dx = \frac{x^4}{4} + C\). Differentiating the result back gives \(\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x} = x^2\), so it checks. The general solution is \(y = \frac{x^3}{4} + \frac{C}{x}\).

Here \(P = \sec x\) and \(Q = \tan x\). Integrating factor \(= e^{\int\sec x\,dx} = e^{\log|\sec x + \tan x|} = \sec x + \tan x\). Then \(y(\sec x + \tan x) = \int \tan x(\sec x + \tan x)\,dx = \int(\sec x\tan x + \sec^2 x - 1)\,dx = \sec x + \tan x - x + C\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(y(\sec x + \tan x) = \sec x + \tan x - x + C\).

Dividing by \(\cos^2 x\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} + (\sec^2 x)\,y = \tan x\sec^2 x\), so \(P = \sec^2 x\) and integrating factor \(= e^{\int\sec^2 x\,dx} = e^{\tan x}\). Then \(y\,e^{\tan x} = \int \tan x\sec^2 x\,e^{\tan x}\,dx\); putting \(t = \tan x\), \(dt = \sec^2 x\,dx\), this is \(\int t\,e^{t}\,dt = e^{t}(t-1) + C = e^{\tan x}(\tan x - 1) + C\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(y = (\tan x - 1) + C\,e^{-\tan x}\).

Dividing by \(x\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2}{x}y = x\log x\), so \(P = \frac{2}{x}\) and integrating factor \(= e^{2\log x} = x^2\). Then \(y\,x^2 = \int x^3\log x\,dx = \frac{x^4}{4}\log x - \int\frac{x^3}{4}\,dx = \frac{x^4}{4}\log x - \frac{x^4}{16} + C\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(y = \frac{x^2}{4}\log x - \frac{x^2}{16} + \frac{C}{x^2}\).

Dividing by \(x\log x\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{1}{x\log x}y = \frac{2}{x^2}\), so \(P = \frac{1}{x\log x}\) and \(\int P\,dx = \log|\log x|\), giving integrating factor \(= \log x\). Then \(y\log x = \int\frac{2\log x}{x^2}\,dx\). By parts, \(\int\frac{\log x}{x^2}\,dx = -\frac{\log x}{x} + \int\frac{dx}{x^2} = -\frac{\log x}{x} - \frac{1}{x}\), so the integral is \(-\frac{2}{x}(\log x + 1) + C\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(y\log x = -\frac{2}{x}(1 + \log x) + C\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(y = (1+x)^{-1}\log|\sin x| + C(1+x^2)^{-1}\); the first factor has lost its exponent and should read \((1+x^2)^{-1}\). As printed the expression does not satisfy the equation for any \(C\). The key’s own second term carries the correct \((1+x^2)\).] Dividing by \((1+x^2)\,dx\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}y = \frac{\cot x}{1+x^2}\), so \(P = \frac{2x}{1+x^2}\) and integrating factor \(= e^{\log(1+x^2)} = 1+x^2\). Then \(y(1+x^2) = \int\frac{\cot x}{1+x^2}(1+x^2)\,dx = \int\cot x\,dx = \log|\sin x| + C\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(y = \frac{\log|\sin x| + C}{1+x^2}\).

Dividing by \(x\) and rearranging, \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(\frac{1}{x} + \cot x\right)y = 1\), so \(P = \frac{1}{x}+\cot x\) and \(\int P\,dx = \log|x| + \log|\sin x|\), giving integrating factor \(= x\sin x\). Then \(y\,x\sin x = \int x\sin x\,dx = -x\cos x + \sin x + C\). Dividing by \(x\sin x\) and differentiating back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(y = \frac{1}{x} - \cot x + \frac{C}{x\sin x}\).

The equation is not linear in \(y\), but writing \(\frac{dx}{dy} = x + y\) it is linear in \(x\) as the dependent variable: \(\frac{dx}{dy} - x = y\), so \(P_1 = -1\) and integrating factor \(= e^{\int(-1)dy} = e^{-y}\). Then \(x\,e^{-y} = \int y\,e^{-y}\,dy = -y\,e^{-y} - e^{-y} + C\). Multiplying by \(e^{y}\), \(x = -y - 1 + C\,e^{y}\). Differentiating back gives \(\frac{dx}{dy} = -1 + C e^{y} = x + y\), so it checks. The general solution is \(x + y + 1 = C\,e^{y}\).

Rearranging, \(y\frac{dx}{dy} + x = y^2\), i.e. \(\frac{dx}{dy} + \frac{1}{y}x = y\), which is linear in \(x\) as the dependent variable with \(P_1 = \frac{1}{y}\). Integrating factor \(= e^{\int\frac{1}{y}dy} = e^{\log y} = y\). Then \(x\,y = \int y\cdot y\,dy = \frac{y^3}{3} + C\). Differentiating back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(x = \frac{y^2}{3} + \frac{C}{y}\).

Writing \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{x+3y^2}{y}\), the equation is linear in \(x\) as the dependent variable: \(\frac{dx}{dy} - \frac{1}{y}x = 3y\), so \(P_1 = -\frac{1}{y}\) and integrating factor \(= e^{-\log y} = \frac{1}{y}\) (using \(y > 0\)). Then \(\frac{x}{y} = \int 3y\cdot\frac{1}{y}\,dy = 3y + C\). Differentiating back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The general solution is \(x = 3y^2 + Cy\).

Here \(P = 2\tan x\) and \(Q = \sin x\). Integrating factor \(= e^{2\int\tan x\,dx} = e^{2\log|\sec x|} = \sec^2 x\). Then \(y\sec^2 x = \int\sin x\sec^2 x\,dx = \int\frac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,dx = \sec x + C\). Putting \(y = 0\) when \(x = \frac{\pi}{3}\): \(0 = \sec\frac{\pi}{3} + C = 2 + C\), so \(C = -2\). Hence \(y\sec^2 x = \sec x - 2\). Multiplying by \(\cos^2 x\) and differentiating back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The particular solution is \(y = \cos x - 2\cos^2 x\).

Dividing by \((1+x^2)\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}y = \frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2}\), so \(P = \frac{2x}{1+x^2}\) and integrating factor \(= e^{\log(1+x^2)} = 1+x^2\). Then \(y(1+x^2) = \int\frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \tan^{-1}x + C\). Putting \(y = 0\) when \(x = 1\): \(0 = \frac{\pi}{4} + C\), so \(C = -\frac{\pi}{4}\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The particular solution is \(y(1+x^2) = \tan^{-1}x - \frac{\pi}{4}\).

Here \(P = -3\cot x\) and \(Q = \sin 2x\). Integrating factor \(= e^{-3\int\cot x\,dx} = e^{-3\log|\sin x|} = \operatorname{cosec}^3 x\). Then \(y\operatorname{cosec}^3 x = \int\frac{\sin 2x}{\sin^3 x}\,dx = \int\frac{2\cos x}{\sin^2 x}\,dx = -\frac{2}{\sin x} + C\), so \(y = -2\sin^2 x + C\sin^3 x\). Putting \(y = 2\) when \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(2 = -2 + C\), so \(C = 4\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The particular solution is \(y = 4\sin^3 x - 2\sin^2 x\).

The slope condition gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y\), i.e. \(\frac{dy}{dx} - y = x\), which is linear with \(P = -1\) and integrating factor \(= e^{-x}\). Then \(y\,e^{-x} = \int x\,e^{-x}\,dx = -x\,e^{-x} - e^{-x} + C\), so \(y = -x - 1 + C\,e^{x}\). The curve passes through \((0,0)\): \(0 = -1 + C\), so \(C = 1\). Checking, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x} - 1 = x + y\). The required curve is \(y = e^{x} - x - 1\), that is \(x + y + 1 = e^{x}\).

The condition "the sum of the coordinates exceeds the slope by 5" gives \(x + y = \frac{dy}{dx} + 5\), i.e. \(\frac{dy}{dx} - y = x - 5\), which is linear with \(P = -1\) and integrating factor \(= e^{-x}\). Then \(y\,e^{-x} = \int(x-5)e^{-x}\,dx = -(x-5)e^{-x} - e^{-x} + C = -(x-4)e^{-x} + C\), so \(y = 4 - x + C\,e^{x}\). The curve passes through \((0,2)\): \(2 = 4 + C\), so \(C = -2\). Checking, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -1 - 2e^{x}\) and \(x+y-5 = x + 4 - x - 2e^{x} - 5 = -1 - 2e^{x}\), which agree. The required curve is \(y = 4 - x - 2e^{x}\).

Writing the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^3 - 3xy^2}{y^3 - 3x^2y}\), numerator and denominator are both homogeneous of degree 3, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\): the factor \(x^3\) cancels and \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1-3v^2}{v^3-3v}\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1-3v^2 - v^4 + 3v^2}{v^3-3v} = \frac{1-v^4}{v^3-3v}\). Separating, \(\frac{v^3-3v}{1-v^4}\,dv = \frac{dx}{x}\). Put \(t = v^2\), \(dt = 2v\,dv\): the left side becomes \(\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{t-3}{(1-t)(1+t)}\,dt = \frac{1}{2}\int\left(\frac{-1}{1-t} - \frac{2}{1+t}\right)dt = \frac{1}{2}\log|1-t| - \log|1+t|\). Hence \(\log|1-v^2| - 2\log(1+v^2) = 2\log|x| + C_1\), i.e. \(\frac{1-v^2}{(1+v^2)^2} = c\,x^2\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), \(1-v^2 = \frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2}\) and \((1+v^2)^2 = \frac{(x^2+y^2)^2}{x^4}\), so \(\frac{x^2(x^2-y^2)}{(x^2+y^2)^2} = c\,x^2\). Cancelling \(x^2\) gives \(x^2 - y^2 = c\,(x^2+y^2)^2\), which is the required general solution.

Since \(x/y\) occurs throughout, treat \(x\) as the dependent variable: \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{x\,e^{x/y} + y^2}{y\,e^{x/y}} = \frac{x}{y} + y\,e^{-x/y}\). Put \(x = vy\), \(\frac{dx}{dy} = v + y\frac{dv}{dy}\): \(v + y\frac{dv}{dy} = v + y\,e^{-v}\), so \(y\frac{dv}{dy} = y\,e^{-v}\), i.e. \(e^{v}\,dv = dy\). Integrating, \(e^{v} = y + C\). Back-substituting \(v = \frac{x}{y}\) and differentiating implicitly gives \(e^{x/y}\frac{y\,dx - x\,dy}{y^2} = dy\), i.e. \(y\,e^{x/y}\,dx = \left(x\,e^{x/y} + y^2\right)dy\), so it checks. The solution is \(e^{x/y} = y + C\).
_note: The equation is not homogeneous in the strict degree sense (the term y^2 has degree 2 while x*e^(x/y) has degree 1), but it still separates under the same substitution x = vy, which is why it sits with the homogeneous group. Solved as printed; no defect implied.

solution: Taking the reciprocal of both sides, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}} - \frac{y}{\sqrt{x}}\), i.e. \(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,y = \frac{e^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\), which is linear with \(P = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\). Since \(\int x^{-1/2}dx = 2\sqrt{x}\), the integrating factor is \(e^{2\sqrt{x}}\). Then \(y\,e^{2\sqrt{x}} = \int e^{2\sqrt{x}}\cdot\frac{e^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx = \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = 2\sqrt{x} + C\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The solution is \(y\,e^{2\sqrt{x}} = 2\sqrt{x} + C\).

Here \(P = \cot x\) and \(Q = 4x\operatorname{cosec} x\). Integrating factor \(= e^{\int\cot x\,dx} = e^{\log|\sin x|} = \sin x\). Then \(y\sin x = \int 4x\operatorname{cosec} x\cdot\sin x\,dx = \int 4x\,dx = 2x^2 + C\). Putting \(y = 0\) when \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(0 = 2\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{4} + C\), so \(C = -\frac{\pi^2}{2}\). Differentiating the result back reproduces the equation, so it checks. The particular solution is \(y\sin x = 2x^2 - \frac{\pi^2}{2}\).
